record.original_question: How can submodels for gene regulation, metabolism, the cell cycle, mechanics, electrophysiology, and transport be linked into modular multiscale or whole-cell models that remain thermodynamically consistent across interfaces, especially when conservation laws and bond-graph structure must be respected?

evidence.quote: Here we will build on this work and extend it to develop whole cell models.
The critical point in model development is to link up sub-models of, for example, gene regulation, metabolism, and the cell cycle.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Develop a mathematical framework for coupling submodels of distinct cellular processes — gene regulation, metabolism, the cell cycle, mechanics, electrophysiology, and transport — into a single multiscale or whole-cell model that satisfies the following requirements:

(i) Each submodel is described as an open dynamical system that exchanges energy and matter with its environment through well-defined interface variables (effort/flow pairs in the sense of bond graphs, e.g., chemical potential and molar flow, voltage and current, force and velocity).

(ii) Each submodel is individually thermodynamically consistent: its constitutive relations derive from a free-energy (or entropy) potential so that, in isolation, it satisfies the first and second laws of thermodynamics and respects mass, charge, and energy conservation laws.

(iii) When any finite collection of these submodels is interconnected by identifying compatible interface variables, the resulting composite system is again thermodynamically consistent and continues to respect all conservation laws — i.e., consistency is preserved under composition (modularity).

(iv) The construction must accommodate the multiple time scales (fast biochemical kinetics, slower regulatory dynamics, cell-cycle and mechanical scales) and the heterogeneous formalisms (ODE chemical kinetics, stoichiometric/flux-balance models, continuum mechanics, cable/Hodgkin–Huxley type equations, reaction–diffusion transport) found across the submodels, possibly via principled model-reduction operations that themselves preserve thermodynamic consistency.

Problem: Construct such a compositional, thermodynamically-consistent modular framework (specifying admissible interfaces, composition rules, and reduction operations), and prove that arbitrary interconnections of submodels drawn from the above classes yield whole-cell models obeying the first and second laws together with all relevant conservation laws.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent work on bond-graph approaches to systems biology (e.g., Gawthrop, Pan, Crampin and collaborators, 2021–2025) has established modular, thermodynamically consistent formulations that unify stoichiometry, thermodynamics and kinetics for biochemical networks, and has begun coupling gene-regulation submodels to metabolic submodels with built-in resource competition and retroactivity. However, a fully general framework spanning all listed domains (cell cycle, mechanics, electrophysiology, transport) within a single whole-cell model, together with consistency-preserving reductions across scales, remains an active research goal rather than a completed result.

status_evidence.title: Modular dynamic biomolecular modelling with bond graphs
status_evidence.snippet: Bond graphs unify stoichiometry, thermodynamics, kinetics and data; modular approach intrinsically enforces thermodynamic constraints and couples metabolism with gene regulation.
status_evidence.claim: Partial progress: bond-graph framework already provides thermodynamically consistent modular coupling for biochemical submodels including metabolism and gene expression.

status_evidence.title: Thermodynamically-consistent, reduced models of gene regulatory networks
status_evidence.snippet: Develops thermodynamically consistent reduced bond-graph models of gene regulatory networks suitable for incorporation into larger systems.
status_evidence.claim: Consistency-preserving reductions exist for gene-regulation submodels, indicating progress but not yet a full whole-cell framework.

status_evidence.title: Modular assembly of dynamic models in systems biology
status_evidence.snippet: Review of modular assembly approaches noting open challenges in coupling heterogeneous submodels while preserving physical consistency.
status_evidence.claim: The complete program of modular thermodynamic linkage across all cellular subsystems remains open.
